questions.base_rate_used: Scenario page base rate: 0 downgrades in 36 recorded S&P actions on EU sovereigns with a stable outlook going in (0%, and 0% as a lower bound on the wider count). S&P usually moves the outlook to negative before it cuts, so I start near zero and allow a small tail for an off-pattern cut.

factors.text: The reference class is clean on this point. S&P has not cut any of these six EU sovereigns straight from a stable outlook since 2014. The normal path is an outlook change first, and an outlook change alone resolves NO. This is the main reason I sit well below the market.

The fiscal and political backdrop is getting worse, which gives S&P cover to act. HCFP calls the 1.0% growth forecast optimistic and sees debt rising toward about 122%. Budget adoption by 31 December is close to a coin flip (50.5% and 49%). Marine Le Pen is priced at 41.1% to win in 2027. The OAT-Bund spread widened from 81.5bp to 96.7bp on the monthly series. This mostly argues for a negative outlook, but it keeps a direct cut possible.

Where the crowd may share an error: the 26.5% Polymarket price trades on thin volume (7345). The 31% Kalshi contract covers any agency through year-end, so it is wider than this question. Both seem to treat a bad fiscal story as if it meant an S&P cut on 27 Nov, and skip the outlook-first habit. The spread series is a degraded monthly average, and no gauge here is tested as a lead on rating actions.

questions.what_would_change_view: Any of these before 27 Nov would push me up toward the market: the government falls on a censure motion, PLF 2027 is rejected at first reading so a special law becomes the base case, or the government raises its 2026 deficit estimate. A confirmation that S&P's current outlook is already negative, not stable, would also break the reference class. A quiet first reading with the revenue part passed would push me toward affirm_stable.
questions.most_likely_wrong: The 'stable outlook going in' premise could be wrong, or S&P could decide that political paralysis before the 2027 election justifies an off-pattern cut. In either case the 0% reference class does not apply and the market's roughly one-in-four is closer to right.
questions.title: S&P review of France, 27 Nov 2026

questions.base_rate_used: The scenario page gives 19 of 21 budgets promulgated by 31 December (90.5%) across 2006-2026. I give more weight to the subset since France lost its majority in 2022. The page shows that subset separately but does not quote it. Its branch notes say the 2024 and 2025 cycles both ended with a special law. The most relevant starting point is therefore roughly a coin flip for a minority government, well below 90.5%.

factors.text: Structural: a minority government since the 2024 dissolution. The last two budget cycles both missed 31 December and ended with a special law, the 2024 and 2025 pattern noted on the scenario page. The full-sample base rate of 90.5% mostly comes from years with a majority.

This budget is politically harder than usual. It has about 54 billion euros of consolidation, including a freeze of basic pensions and of the civil-service pay index. It lands just before the spring 2027 presidential race, in which Le Pen has launched her campaign and is priced at 41.1%. Opposition parties gain little from letting it pass, and a 49.3 invites a censure vote.

The government has tools to force it through. Kalshi prices use of Article 49.3 on the budget in 2026 at 66%. The Article 47 deadline of 10 December also opens a never-used ordinance route. This keeps the chance of adoption well above zero, provided the government survives.

questions.what_would_change_view: I would move up if PS or LR publicly commit not to censure a 49.3 text, or if a joint committee agreement is reached in mid-December. I would move down if a censure motion gathers PS votes, if the revenue part fails at first reading in November, or if the government signals a special law as in 2024 and 2025.
questions.most_likely_wrong: Prediction markets at 50.5% and 49% may be right. The government may have secured a quiet non-censure deal, like the one that eventually passed the 2026 budget, and simply land it before Christmas this time, given the reputational cost of a third consecutive special law. My pre-election pessimism could then be overdone. The market signals themselves carry little tested evidence, and the official-optimism gauge is untested.
questions.title: France 2027 budget and the Article 47 deadline

questions.base_rate_used: The scenario page has no computed probability for an RN win. Its reference class says the final-poll leader won 4 of 4 presidential run-offs, with an RMS poll error of 5.78 pp. That only helps once final polls exist, and the snapshot holds no polls six months out. As a last resort I start from market prices: on Polymarket, Le Pen at 41.1% plus Bardella at 1.7%; on Kalshi, Le Pen at 45% plus Bardella at 1.4%. Together that puts the RN candidate in the low-to-mid 40s.

factors.text: Markets price the RN candidate highest among single candidates. Le Pen has formally launched her campaign, and headlines are framing the race as hers to lose. That keeps the starting point near the market level. Note that the market splits RN odds between Le Pen and Bardella as though her ineligibility case were mostly settled; the question counts either name, so that split does not change the YES side.

The centre-right side is split across Lisnard at 19.6%, Philippe at 14.5%, Lagarde at 4.2% and others, and together they are close to the RN total. A run-off is usually a two-way race in which non-RN voters consolidate, and the signposts say that consolidation (withdrawals, sponsorship totals in March 2027) has not happened yet. I shade slightly below the market because fragmented anti-RN odds tend to understate the eventual run-off opponent.

The crowd's main gauge carries little evidential weight. The poll-versus-prediction-market gap is badged tested_no_lead, and prediction-market series in general are tested_no_lead. These markets have high volume but are untested as forecasters this far out. Fiscal strain could still feed the anti-incumbent vote: HCFP expects debt to rise toward about 122% of GDP and sees the 2029 deficit target as very unlikely to be met.

questions.what_would_change_view: I would move up if second-round polls against the leading centre-right candidate show RN ahead by more than the 5.78 pp historical poll error, or if the centre-right stays split into March 2027. I would move down if one centre-right candidate consolidates (the others withdraw) and run-off polls show RN behind. A ruling that keeps Le Pen off the ballot would matter only if Bardella polled weaker than her.
questions.most_likely_wrong: I may be underrating RN. The old pattern of anti-RN voters uniting in the run-off may have weakened enough, under fiscal austerity and a polarised climate, that the market's low-to-mid 40s is too low rather than too high.
questions.title: France 2027 presidential election

questions.base_rate_used: The scenario page has no computed base rate; em-macro records no Brazilian fiscal-target revisions. My starting point is the page's context: Brazil cut a self-set primary target in July 2015 (mid-year, under fiscal stress) and in April 2024 (the following year's target, inside the PLDO). That suggests revisions are a real risk, but they usually come with the April budget-guidelines cycle, after this question's 31 March window closes. I start near 70% that the target and rule survive to 31 March.

factors.text: The government's own 2027 budget bill says the framework is met. It shows a counted surplus of R$83.4 billion against a R$73.2 billion target, and the target has a tolerance band of 0.25 point of GDP either side. A re-elected government entering its new term on 5 January has little reason to formally cut a target it claims to be meeting within its first three months. The more natural place to move goalposts is the April budget-guidelines cycle, which falls outside the window.

Independent estimates sit far from the target. IFI puts the counted 2027 result at only R$0.9 billion, below even the lower tolerance bound, and says about R$35.7 billion of spending would have to be frozen. IFI also sees a potential 2027 deficit of 1.0% of GDP. The Focus 2027 median is -0.3% of GDP against the 0.5% target, though that dispersion gauge is untested. A spending freeze of that size early in a new term is politically hard, so the first bimonthly report around 22 March could instead propose a change.

Markets already treat the post-run-off fiscal path as at risk. USD/BRL rose 7.61% in the week to 30 October, and the DI Jan-29 proxy rose from 12.81% to 14.86%. This cuts both ways. It raises the chance that fiscal looseness is the plan. It also gives the finance team a strong reason to defend the formal target in the short run, as the BCB's FX swap rollovers show officials managing stress rather than adding to it.

questions.what_would_change_view: I would move down if the December PLOA or LDO vote changes the 2027 target, or if a PLP is floated to alter the LC 200/2023 limits. I would also move down if the January finance-minister pick signals a framework rewrite, or if ministers publicly question the 0.5% target. I would move up if the PLOA passes in December without new exclusions and the Focus 2027 primary median moves toward the target.
questions.most_likely_wrong: The crowd's error may be treating 'will miss the target' as the same as 'will change the target'. Focus and IFI forecasts measure the first; this question resolves on the second, which is one reason I stay above even odds. My most likely error runs the other way: the LDO 2027 may still be open in Congress during the December budget session. That would let the target be lowered quietly by amendment before the window even starts in earnest, which my April-timing argument does not cover.
questions.title: Brazil 2027: fiscal-framework credibility

questions.base_rate_used: The scenario page has no direct base rate for keeping two-thirds. Its reference class (Mexico's midterms in 2009, 2015 and 2021) says only that the final-poll leader won 3 of 3, with an RMS poll error of 4.12 pp. The closest precedent is 2021, when the governing coalition kept its majority but lost two-thirds. My starting point is that a midterm usually trims the governing bloc and that holding 334 of 500 seats is the harder outcome. That puts the start somewhat below even.

factors.text: Reference-class pull downward: in the one recent midterm of a dominant governing coalition (2021) it kept its majority but lost two-thirds. The page's signpost says two-thirds needs roughly 55% of the vote plus the over-representation cap, a high bar to clear twice in a row.

Morena's dominance is not in doubt: Polymarket gives it 86.6% and Kalshi 86% to win the most seats. In 2024 Sheinbaum beat her 17 pp poll lead by winning by 33 pp, so polls have recently understated this coalition. But these markets are related-only (most seats, not two-thirds), and prediction-market gauges are tested_no_lead, so they get little weight.

The vote is seven months away, and the page notes poll errors are larger that far out than the 4.12 pp final-poll figure. The seat count also depends on INE's over-representation rulings, which a headline poll margin cannot capture (em-macro's 2024 lesson). That widens the spread of outcomes rather than shifting the centre.

questions.what_would_change_view: I would move up if early-2027 polls put the coalition's vote share above 55%, or if INE signals it will apply over-representation as leniently as in 2024. I would move down if PAN-PRI or MC form district alliances, or if coalition polling falls into the 45-55% band. The crowd's likely shared error is reading the 86.6% 'most seats' price as confidence in two-thirds. Those are different questions, and the gap between them is where the market risk sits (the 2024 peso fell sharply on the supermajority, not the presidency).
questions.most_likely_wrong: Sheinbaum's popularity and a fragmented opposition could repeat 2024. The coalition's vote share and INE's seat formula could then deliver two-thirds comfortably, as when polls understated Morena's margin by a wide amount in 2024.
questions.title: Mexico midterms, 6 Jun 2027

questions.base_rate_used: The scenario page has no computed base rate: this is the agreement's first review cycle and em-macro has no trade-agreement events. I start from the nearest market price, Polymarket's 8.5% for an extension in 2026 (pm:2761052). That market covers the earlier review, not this question. The scenario's own event note implies the 2026 review ended without an extension. I then widen the starting point for the extra time to 1 July 2027.

factors.text: At the first chance to extend, in 2026, the crowd gave only 8.5% to an extension. The default under art. 34.7 is a cycle of annual reviews, so the US keeps the review as standing leverage. YES needs all three governments to confirm in writing, which is a high bar, and the default favours the annual branch.

Kalshi gives 24% to a trilateral revised deal in 2026. A revised text is the most natural vehicle for an extension, and recent USTR releases show the US and Mexico settling disputes cooperatively (Rapid Response labour case, Minera Peñasquito remediation). That keeps extension a live path rather than a tail.

US trade decisions often arrive off-calendar. Mexico's June 2027 midterms fall just before the 1 July review, and Morena's possible supermajority is itself a US concern. Both give Washington reasons to hold back a 16-year commitment until after the vote.

questions.what_would_change_view: I would move up if USTR's consultation report recommends extension, if US tariffs on Mexican goods are cut below 10%, or if a trilateral revised text is signed. Any of these would make a written confirmation by 1 July 2027 plausible. I would move down toward the bilateral or withdrawal branches if the US proposes separate US-Mexico and US-Canada texts, or if officials describe withdrawal as leverage. A collapse of the next US-Mexico bilateral round (placeholder date 30 November) would also push me down.
questions.most_likely_wrong: A political deal arrives as a package: tariff relief plus a revised text, signed with a 16-year extension before the US 2028 cycle. In that case thin, related-only markets and my status-quo default understate how quickly an extension can be granted once the US has extracted concessions.
questions.title: USMCA annual review, 1 Jul 2027

week_change.text: USD/BRL PTAX is up from 5.0377 on 2026-10-23 to 5.4212 on 2026-10-30, a 7.61% rise.
DI Jan-29 proxy is up from 12.81% to 14.86% over the week, and DI Jan-31 proxy from 12.91% to 15.17%.
The Prefixado 10-year proxy is up from 13.03% to 15.06%, and the IPCA+ longest proxy from 6.7% to 7.37%.
Focus year-end 2027 Selic median is 11.75%, and the year-end 2026 median is down 0.75 point over three months.

why_it_matters.text: The real has sold off hard since Lula's surprise run-off win. USD/BRL PTAX rose from 5.0377 on 23 Oct to 5.4212 on 30 Oct, a 7.61% fall in the real. em-macro's hold-out test found that election currency moves continued rather than reversed. The fade-the-day-1 rule lost money on Brazil's 2022 run-off. So do not assume this move will bounce back on its own.

The bond repricing sits in the long end, not the short end, which points to fiscal and political risk rather than near-term policy. Over the week the DI Jan-29 proxy rose 205bp to 14.86%, the Jan-31 proxy rose 226bp to 15.17% and the 10-year Prefixado proxy rose 203bp to 15.06%. The Jan-27 proxy rose only 6bp to 13.51%. The inflation-linked real-rate proxy also rose, from 6.7% to 7.37%, so investors are demanding more real compensation, not just pricing higher inflation. In em-macro's fit sample, bond moves after elections tended to continue.

The 3-4 Nov Copom is the central bank's first response to the shock, and expectations are split. The Focus median for the meeting is 13.5%, a cut from the 13.75% Selic, but it was collected on 23 Oct, before the run-off. Prediction markets give 22.5% to a 25bp cut (Polymarket) and 23% to a hike of more than 25bp (Kalshi). em-macro found Brazil's real responds to Copom surprises within days. But rate-surprise regressions added almost nothing out of sample, so the decision may matter less for the real than the fiscal message.

The fiscal gap is the underlying driver for long bonds. The government says the 2027 budget's counted surplus is R$83.4 billion against a R$73.2 billion target. IFI says it would be only R$0.9 billion and that about R$35.7 billion of spending would need freezing. The Focus 2027 primary-balance median is -0.3% of GDP against the 0.5% target, and IFI sees a potential 2027 deficit of 1.0% of GDP. The 2027 fiscal-framework scenario has no computed base rate.

The central bank has announced only traditional FX swap auctions to roll over contracts maturing 1 December. That is a rollover of existing protection, not fresh intervention. Any move to add new swaps would signal concern about the real's slide.

watch.what_to_watch: This is the first Focus survey taken fully after the run-off. Watch whether the next-Copom median moves off 13.5%, and whether the year-end 2026 (13.25%) and 2027 (11.75%) Selic medians rise. Watch whether the 2027 primary-balance median slips below -0.3% of GDP and whether 2027 inflation expectations (4.34%) rise. A jump in dispersion matters: this gauge has a tested record of flagging when the decision differs from the survey median.

Hold, cut or hike from 13.75%, and above all the statement. Look for language on fiscal risk, on the weaker real feeding into prices, and on guidance for 9 December. A cut into a 7.61% currency slide would risk looking like political accommodation. A hold with hawkish guidance is the outcome markets seem least prepared for, given Focus still showed a cut. Judge the real's reaction over several days, not just the first session.

How the Copom outcome feeds into Focus. Does the year-end 2026 Selic median move toward the current 13.75%? Does the 2027 median of 11.75% start to rise? Does 2026 inflation expectation (5.19%) move up as the weaker real passes through?
The fiscal lines: the 2027 primary-balance median (-0.3%) and the 2027 overall-balance median (-8.5%). A fall in the primary median is a signpost for the target-cut branch of the fiscal scenario.

Whether the Treasury freezes spending to protect the 2026 target, given IFI expects a 0.5% of GDP deficit and Focus a -0.48% primary balance. Also watch any revision to revenue and growth assumptions that feed the 2027 budget, which IFI says rests on optimistic inputs. A meaningful freeze would support the credible branch. A missing freeze or new exclusions would support the exclusions or target-cut branches.

Whether the 2027 primary-balance median keeps drifting and whether the dispersion of Selic forecasts widens before December. Wider disagreement raises the odds that the 9 December decision differs from the survey median.

This is the last read before the 9 December Copom. Compare the Selic median for that meeting with the DI Jan-27 proxy (13.51% on 29 Oct). Also check whether inflation expectations for 2027 have moved away from 4.34% as the weaker real feeds through.

risks.text: A dovish Copom surprise read as political accommodation could extend the real's slide. A large hike could flatten the curve without restoring fiscal confidence. Prediction markets price both tails, a 22.5% cut chance and a 23% chance of a hike above 25bp.

The re-elected government could signal looser fiscal rules or new exclusions before the December budget vote. The November 2024 analog for a target cut is a 112bp rise in the DI Jan-29 proxy and a 4.39% rise in USD/BRL within three trading days. That would come on top of a repricing that has already happened.

The election result is being contested: Bolsonaro is contesting and has reportedly sought an annulment. Markets put annulment by 31 December at only 3.2%, but prolonged contestation could keep a political premium in the long end.
The US backdrop could add pressure. The US 10-year is at 4.98% and the US midterms are on 3 November. A rise in US yields would weigh on the real through the external channel.
The bond readings are degraded proxies. Tesouro LTN yields stand in for the B3 DI curve, so the true curve move may differ in size.

consensus.view: Surveys and markets disagree, and the survey is stale. The 23 Oct Focus, taken before the run-off, expects a cut to 13.5% at this meeting and 13.25% by year-end 2026. It also expects 11.75% by end-2027, 2027 inflation of 4.34% and a 2027 primary balance of -0.3% of GDP against the 0.5% target. The government says its 2027 budget counts a surplus above target. IFI disputes this. Prediction markets have moved away from the Focus cut: Polymarket gives a 25bp cut 22.5%, and Kalshi gives a hike above 25bp 23%. Kalshi puts 67% on exactly 5 cuts in 2026 and 11% on 7 or more. Leveraged-fund BRL futures positioning sits at the 67.3rd percentile, but that gauge has tested with no lead, so it deserves little weight.

judgement.might_be_wrong: The shared error may be treating Copom as the lever that settles the real. Analysts, the press and prediction markets all frame the next weeks around the Selic. But em-macro's hold-out shows rate decisions have become quieter, and rate surprises explain little of later currency moves. The repricing sits in the long end and real yields, not the 13.51% Jan-27 proxy, which still sits below the 13.75% Selic. So the market itself says the problem is fiscal, not the policy rate. If so, neither a hike nor a hold will stop the move. What matters is whether the 20 November bimonthly report and the December budget close the gap between the government's R$83.4 billion counted surplus and IFI's R$0.9 billion. Focus's 2027 primary median even improved by 0.1 point over three months, which suggests forecasters may be anchoring on the official numbers. The opposite error is also possible. The hold-out found election currency moves continued, but on only 14 trades. If the government quickly names a credible finance team, the long end could retrace faster than the momentum evidence implies. Prediction-market signals are tested with no lead, so their hike pricing may be noise rather than information.

upcoming.title: Chamber of Deputies deadline to approve the 2027 spending budget (PEF)
USMCA: US-Mexico bilateral round (next round not announced)

why_it_matters.text: The peso has been calm while Brazil's real was hit. USD/MXN rose only 0.69% in the week to 18.7962, against a 7.61% jump in USD/BRL after Brazil's run-off. Investors are treating Mexico as separate from Brazil's fiscal scare. That holds only while Mexico's own fiscal and trade stories stay quiet.

Banxico's 6.5% policy rate against an effective US fed funds rate of 3.88% is the carry that keeps investors holding pesos. Leveraged funds are already net long MXN at the 79.5th percentile (24.5% of open interest). A surprise cut on 5 November would trim that carry. The positioning gauge is badged tested_no_lead, so it says how crowded the trade is, not which way the peso goes next.

Local bonds have been rallying. The 10-year Mbono auction yield fell 10bp to 9.25% while the US 10-year sits at 4.98%. In em-macro's 2005–2021 sample, Mexican 10-year yields moved about half a basis point per basis point of rate surprise. Out of sample, rate-surprise effects added almost nothing, so do not lean on a big bond reaction to Banxico.

The 2027 budget only narrows the broad deficit (RFSP) from 4.1% to 3.9% of GDP, against 3.5% planned in April. It still pays Pemex 81.1 billion pesos. México Evalúa says hitting even that relies on record tax collection and is not enough to stabilise debt. For bonds this is a slow-burning supply and rating risk rather than a 30-day shock. KBRA has just affirmed BBB stable.

watch.what_to_watch: Whether the 2026 year-end inflation median keeps falling from 3.87%. Whether the 2026 Q4 policy-rate median stays at 6.5%; in the last survey nobody forecast a cut by year end, with a range of 6.5 to 6.75. If some economists now pencil in a cut, the 16.6–18% market odds for 5 November look less like a long shot.

Markets price a hold at 81–83.5%. A hold with neutral guidance should be a non-event, since holds barely move currencies in em-macro. Watch the vote split and whether the statement opens the door to cuts as inflation expectations fall. A surprise cut would mostly show up in the peso's carry appeal. TIIE 28-day edging up to 6.8061% shows money markets are not leaning toward a cut.

Whether the Chamber passes the spending budget on time without adding spending. Whether Pemex support stays at 81.1 billion pesos or creeps up. Whether the RFSP path of 3.9% of GDP survives intact. Late changes that raise borrowing would matter more for Mbonos than for the peso.
watch.event: Chamber of Deputies deadline to approve the 2027 spending budget (PEF)

watch.what_to_watch: The date is only a placeholder. Watch for USTR or Economía announcing an actual round, and above all for US tariff statements that arrive with no calendar warning. Markets give a USMCA extension in 2026 only 8.5% and a trilateral revised deal 24%, so any talk of separate bilateral texts or withdrawal is the peso's biggest tail risk.
watch.event: USMCA: US-Mexico bilateral round (next round not announced)

watch.what_to_watch: How economists revise after the 5 November decision and the budget vote. Watch the 2027 policy-rate median (6.5%, range 5.75 to 7.25), the 2027 public-sector balance median (-3.7% of GDP) and 2027 growth (1.8%). Growth sliding toward the bottom of the budget's 1.5% to 2.5% range would undercut its revenue assumptions.

risks.text: US trade shock outside the calendar. A move toward bilateral deals or a withdrawal notice is the scenario with the largest peso downside; the 2016 analog saw USD/MXN rise 13.74% in three days. The US midterms on 3 November may also change the tone of trade policy.

Crowded long-peso positioning meets an EM sell-off. Brazil's currency and bond rout could spread if global investors cut emerging-market risk across the board, and a positioning gauge at the 79.5th percentile leaves room to unwind.

Fiscal slippage. IMEF notes the 2025 broad deficit came in at 4.8% against 3.9% planned, and the 2027 plan again depends on revenue and on a Pemex that lost 28 billion pesos in the first half of 2026. A repeat miss would bring rating pressure back.

A dovish Banxico surprise. Survey inflation expectations fell 0.33 point in three months, which gives Banxico cover to cut before the survey consensus expects. That would weaken the carry case for the peso.

consensus.view: Steady as she goes. Prediction markets price a Banxico hold at 81–83.5% on 5 November. The Banxico survey has the policy rate at 6.5% at the end of both 2026 and 2027, with 2026 inflation at 3.87% and falling. The fiscal package is read as a modest tightening (RFSP from 4.1% to 3.9%), and KBRA affirmed BBB stable. Markets give Morena 86.6% to win the most seats in 2027. Positioning is long the peso, and the currency has barely reacted to Brazil's turmoil.

judgement.might_be_wrong: The shared assumption is that Mexico is insulated: carry plus a Morena-dominated, predictable politics plus a quiet calendar. Three weak points stand out. First, the dangers are largely unscheduled. US trade decisions do not wait for the placeholder 30 November round, and the market odds on USMCA outcomes come from thin markets. Second, '86.6% Morena wins most seats' answers the wrong question. In 2024 the peso fell because of a congressional supermajority, which a headline winner or two-candidate margin cannot capture. A crowd comfortable with Morena winning may be mispricing the two-thirds outcome that hurt in 2024 (USD/MXN +7.21% over five days). Third, survey inflation forecasts have been falling, and the survey and positioning badges are untested or tested_no_lead. So the calm consensus rests on gauges with no proven forecasting value. My confidence is moderate. The most likely way I am wrong is that nothing happens: Banxico holds, the budget passes and carry keeps the peso firm through December.

Article 47 70-day deadline for the PLF 2027 is 10 December 2026; Polymarket puts a 2026 budget adoption at 50.5% and Kalshi at 49%.
Kalshi puts use of Article 49.3 on the 2027 budget in 2026 at 66%.

upcoming.title: Standard & Poor's sovereign rating review: France

why_it_matters.text: The French 10-year spread over Germany widened sharply before the latest budget and rating news. The monthly average rose from 81.5bp in August to 96.7bp in September, and the French 10-year averaged 4.44% against 4.0%. The Bund was 3.38% on 2026-10-30. These are ECB monthly averages that can be up to five weeks old, so any October or November move is not yet visible. The series is also untested as a signal.

The 2027 budget is the main driver of the spread. The bills carry about 54 billion euros of consolidation and aim to cut the deficit from 5.4% of GDP in 2026 to 5.0% in 2027. The fiscal watchdog (HCFP) calls the 1.0% growth assumption optimistic. It says the plan works only if every measure passes, and it sees debt rising toward about 122% of GDP. A minority government must pass all of this, likely through Article 49.3, which invites a censure vote.

S&P reviews France on 27 November. The scenario page's own guesses for the spread are about -2bp for a plain affirmation, +4bp for a move to a negative outlook, and about 12.3bp (range 9.69 to 14.92) for a cut to A. A one-notch S&P cut is unlikely to trigger forced selling, because France would still keep a AA-category rating: Moody's affirmed Aa3 with a negative outlook on 23 October. That Moody's rating is the one reserve managers' thresholds hinge on.

The 2027 presidential race is already a bond story. Polymarket gives Marine Le Pen 41.1% and Kalshi 45%. The closest analog is the June 2024 dissolution, when an RN majority became possible: the spread widened about 17bp in monthly averages. That pressure can build long before the April 2027 vote.

France has no currency of its own, so French stress shows up in the spread to Germany rather than in the euro. EUR/USD was 1.1199 on 2026-10-23, down only 0.28% on the week (an untested series). The ECB's backstop (TPI) is conditional on fiscal compliance, so a failed budget weakens the safety net for French bonds more than it moves the euro.

watch.what_to_watch: Whether S&P keeps France at A+ and, more likely to matter, whether it changes the outlook. Since 2014, S&P has made 0 downgrades in 36 recorded actions on EU sovereigns that went in with a stable outlook. An outlook change would resolve the 'downgrade' markets NO but could still widen the spread. Before the date, watch three things: whether a censure motion succeeds before 27 November, whether the National Assembly passes the revenue part of PLF 2027 at first reading, and whether the government raises its 2026 deficit estimate above 5.4%. Agencies usually publish after the Friday close, so the market reaction comes the following Monday. Our monthly spread series will not show it until the December average is published.
watch.event: Standard & Poor's sovereign rating review: France

risks.text: The government falls on a censure motion over the budget. Kalshi puts use of Article 49.3 in 2026 at 66%, and each use invites a censure vote. When the Barnier government fell in December 2024, the monthly spread rose 4.7bp, which understates the daily move. The modelled effect of losing seat share is 19.08bp (range 9.0 to 29.16).

Ratings pile up rather than arriving singly. S&P reviews on 27 November and KBRA on 11 December, while Moody's Aa3 already carries a negative outlook. A further step by Moody's would threaten France's last AA-category rating, which matters for some reserve managers.

Growth and the deficit could slip. The government assumes 1.0% growth in 2027, against a consensus of 0.81%. The HCFP says downside risks dominate and that the 2029 target of a deficit below 3% is very unlikely to be met.

Election risk could be priced early. Le Pen is at 41.1% on Polymarket and has launched her campaign, and the 2024 RN analog widened the spread about 17bp. The modelled effect of a more populist government is 12.44bp, but its range includes zero.

We cannot see or forecast this market well. The spread data are monthly and lag by weeks. The em-macro spread-mispricing model did far worse than 'no change' for France (error ratio 1.59 at 3 months): it kept expecting the spread to narrow while it widened through 2024–26.

consensus.view: The three official forecasters (IMF, OECD and European Commission) put France's deficit at 5.11% of GDP in 2026 and 5.2% in 2027, slightly worse than the government's 5.0% path for 2027. They put 2027 growth at 0.81%, below the budget's 1.0%. Prediction markets treat the budget as a coin flip: 50.5% on Polymarket and 49% on Kalshi for promulgation by 31 December. That compares with 19 of 21 past budgets promulgated on time, although the special laws of 2024 and 2025 show how the minority era differs. Kalshi gives 66% to Article 49.3. Markets price a downgrade by Moody's or S&P by 30 November at 26.5%, and any agency in 2026 at 31%. Le Pen is at 41.1%. The bond market had already pushed the spread to 96.7bp by September.

judgement.might_be_wrong: The crowd may be making two linked errors. First, the 26.5% price on a downgrade looks high: S&P has made 0 downgrades in 36 recorded actions on EU sovereigns going in with a stable outlook since 2014. The likelier bad outcome is an outlook change to negative, which those markets resolve NO. A NO could be misread as relief even if the spread widens a little. Second, forecasters and markets may share the government's assumption that the budget's measures will pass. The three official forecasters sit only a few tenths away from the government's numbers, and the 'official optimism gap' gauge is untested. The real tail is therefore a censure-driven special law and a further slide in growth, not the S&P date itself. Treat all of these market prices with caution: the evidence badges mark prediction markets as tested_no_lead and the French spread series as untested. History also argues against betting on a reversal. Models that called the French spread too wide failed out of sample, so 'it has widened enough' is as risky a consensus as 'the downgrade is coming'.

US 2-year Treasury yield fell 6bp to 4.61% on 2026-10-29; the effective fed funds rate is 3.88% and the upper target limit is 4.0%.
The broad US dollar index was 121.3202 on 2026-10-23, down 0.0329.

week_change.text: Gold is down from 4007.90 on 2026-10-23 to 3884.90, a 3.07% fall over the week.
Silver is down from 53.711 to 49.135, an 8.52% fall over the week.
The VIX is down from 19.03 to 17.2 over the week, and the broad dollar index is down from 121.4048 to 121.3202.

why_it_matters.text: Gold's drop this week does not fit the usual explanation. Gold fell 3.07% over the week to 3884.90, including a 146.5 drop on 30 October alone. Over the same week the US 10-year real (TIPS) yield edged down to 2.63%, and the latest broad dollar reading also slipped, to 121.3202. Normally lower real yields and a softer dollar support gold. So something outside rates and the dollar drove the sale.

Silver fell harder, down 8.52% over the week to 49.135. A bigger fall in the more speculative metal points to investors cutting crowded precious-metals positions, not a change in the macro picture. Forced selling of that kind can run further than fundamentals suggest, or reverse sharply.

Central-bank buying, a key pillar of support, slowed. IMF reporters' net purchases fell to 20.34 tonnes in September from 45.76 in August. One month is noisy, but if official demand keeps slowing, gold loses a buyer that does not care about price.

Safe-haven demand is easing. The Geopolitical Risk index fell to 165.253 from 220.838 a week earlier, and the VIX fell from 19.03 to 17.2 over the week. Less fear means less reason to hold gold as insurance.

US Treasury pricing does not point to much Fed easing. The 2-year yield is 4.61%, above the Fed funds upper limit of 4.0% and the effective rate of 3.88%. When short-term yields sit above the policy rate, markets are not betting on rate cuts. That removes one usual tailwind for gold and keeps the 10-year near 4.98%.
The dollar has been flat, at 121.3202 against 121.4048 a week earlier, so it neither explains nor offsets gold's fall. This reading is dated 23 October and is stale. Treat it as backdrop only.

watch.what_to_watch: Watch which party controls the House and Senate, then how the 10-year real yield (now 2.63%) and the dollar react over the following days. A split Congress usually means policy gridlock and few surprises. A sweep that raises worries about deficits could push up long-term yields, including the 10-year at 4.98%. That could hurt gold through higher real yields, or help it if investors seek protection from fiscal risk. The key test: does gold resume falling even if real yields and the dollar do not rise? That would confirm last week's selling was about positioning, not macro.

risks.text: Investors may keep unwinding positions. Silver's 8.52% weekly fall and gold's 146.5 drop in one day suggest forced or crowded selling. That can continue no matter what US rates do.
Central-bank demand may stay weak. If net purchases do not recover from 20.34 tonnes, gold loses its steadiest buyer.
Geopolitical calm may persist. A further fall in the Geopolitical Risk index from 165.253 would drain more safe-haven demand. A fresh spike would do the reverse, and quickly.

Treasury pricing may turn more hawkish after the midterms. With the 2-year at 4.61%, already above the Fed's upper limit of 4.0%, a rise in real yields from 2.63% would add a macro headwind on top of the positioning one.

consensus.view: There is no survey for gold, so the consensus has to be read from models and market prices. The frozen gold-events model expects gold to rise 0.27% and silver to fall 0.71% over the next 5 trading days, in effect calm after the sell-off. That forecast uses data as of 27 October, before the 30 October drop, and has been scored on 0 weeks out of sample. Treasury pricing (2-year at 4.61% against a Fed funds upper limit of 4.0%) implies no near-term easing. The calm VIX of 17.2 suggests markets expect a quiet midterm.

judgement.might_be_wrong: The shared error is likely the assumption that gold is driven mainly by real yields and the dollar, so a midterm that leaves them unchanged leaves gold quiet. That assumption failed last week. Gold fell 3.07% while the TIPS yield and the dollar both edged lower, so the drivers that model, market commentary and the midterm framing all lean on did not explain the move. The likelier drivers are slower central-bank buying (20.34 tonnes against 45.76), fading geopolitical fear and liquidation of crowded positions, which silver's 8.52% fall points to. None of these is on the event calendar. The gold-events model, the closest thing to a forecast, has no out-of-sample record and its data predate the drop, so its call for calm deserves little weight. The most likely way this note is wrong is the reverse: the sale was a one-off flush, and gold rebounds once forced selling ends, whatever the midterm outcome.
